name: Pan American
label: Kranky
lede: Mark Nelson played guitar in Labradford, the band Kranky was founded to release, and in 1997 started Pan American for the music that was too electronic for it. He's still at it, with records built around his son's heartbeat and his father's death.

eras.title: A band a label was built for
eras.text: Mark Nelson sang and played guitar in Labradford, the Richmond, Virginia band whose debut gave Kranky a reason to exist. In the summer of 1997 he started a side project for the music that was too electronic for it.

q: The early '90s was arguably peak indie rock, and Labradford were the opposite of that.
years.src: Bandcamp Daily: Kranky Celebrates 25 Years · Chicago Reader: Kranky and Proud of It · Wikipedia: Kranky
years.h: A label gets built so Labradford can have a record
years.p: Joel Leoschke and Bruce Adams, an ex-Touch and Go publicist, start Kranky in Chicago and release Labradford's Prazision LP as catalog number krank 001.
years.xp:
Leoschke worked at the Chicago distributor Cargo, where Labradford's self-released 7-inch landed on his desk. He told Bandcamp Daily the band was "so uncommercial, so unique, and so compelling that it demanded to be paid attention to."

Labradford, with [[Carter Brown|f6aba14e-3ab2-4f4c-b729-814dd97609c7]] and [[Robert Donne|dbcf7f68-2f46-4825-a534-bd6227d00605]], made six albums for Kranky between 1993 and 2001.

yt: Nelson interview, Labradford and Pan American (2024)
years.h: Too electronic for Labradford, so Nelson starts a second project
years.p: That summer he begins Pan American, a solo project of electronics, dub rhythms and guitar, often styled Pan•American. Exclaim! says the material was too electronic for Labradford.
years.xp: Nelson had come to Richmond in the early '90s to attend Virginia Commonwealth University. He told Style Weekly that "Time unfolds there a little differently than elsewhere." Where he lived when Pan American began is unclear in the sources: Style Weekly says he moved to Chicago after Labradford's 2001 hiatus.

eras.title: Dub, and a little help from Low
eras.text: Pan American's first four albums all came out on Kranky, alongside Labradford's last records. By the late 1990s the Labradford members were scattered between Richmond, Washington and Chicago, and Nelson's side project became his main outlet.

years.src: Chicago Reader: Kranky and Proud of It · Wikipedia
years.h: A self-titled debut with dub underneath
years.p: The Chicago Reader heard delicate guitar lines and mournful organ swells laid over dub grooves.

years.h: Rob Mazurek, and Low on one track
years.p: Pan American's second album brings in Chicago cornetist [[Rob Mazurek|73c34525-f9c6-4c33-9abe-007748aaebe5]], and [[Low|42faad37-8aaa-42e4-a300-5a7dae79ed24]]'s [[Alan Sparhawk|36aa434c-6823-44b7-b5a6-53bde476c642]] and [[Mimi Parker|31e0783a-9c5d-4218-9f23-4b9427b111e7]] sing on the track Code.

years.h: Labradford's sixth album turns out to be its last so far
years.p: Fixed::Context is recorded with [[Steve Albini|a4d486bd-6020-4a36-9c7d-bf5ce174bcd1]], and the band goes quiet without announcing a split. Pan American becomes Nelson's main project.

years.h: The River Made No Sound, with Labradford gone quiet
years.p: Pan American's third Kranky album is the first Nelson makes after Labradford's last record.

years.h: Quiet City fills out with Chicago players
years.p: Charles Kim, Vandermark 5 drummer Tim Mulvenna and David Max Crawford play on Pan American's fourth Kranky album.

eras.title: A heartbeat on the record
eras.text: Nelson became a father, and the first Pan American record after that carried the sound of his son before he was born. It came out in Austria, not on Kranky.

years.h: His unborn son's heartbeat runs through every track
years.p: For Waiting, For Chasing, Pan American's fifth album, comes out on the Austrian electronic label Mosz. It is built on field recordings of that heartbeat.

years.cap: Labradford playing in-store at Reckless Records
years.p: White Bird Release is his first Kranky album since Quiet City in 2004.

eras.title: One record as a band, then Anjou
eras.text: For one album Pan American was a real band, with Chicago drummer Steven Hess of Locrian as a full member and Labradford's Robert Donne on bass. The three then became a new Kranky group, Anjou, and Pan American went dormant.

years.cap: Mark Nelson as Pan American at Transmissions V, Ravenna, Italy
years.h: The solo project grows a drummer
years.p: [[Steven Hess|f6e3c48b-fe51-42b0-b002-9d77da680442]] joins as a full member for the first time, with Robert Donne on bass. Fluid Radio heard a band instead of a solo project.

years.h: Anjou takes over, and Pan American goes quiet
years.p: Nelson, Donne and Hess release Anjou on Kranky, after four years of work on digital and analog synths. A second album, Epithymía, follows in 2017.
years.xp: The Chicago Reader later wrote that Pan American went dormant while Nelson worked on Anjou and focused on family. Hess went on to the Chicago duo Cleared with Michael Vallera.

eras.title: A son, a father
eras.text: Pan American came back as Nelson alone, recording at home in Evanston, Illinois, with guitars and a hammered dulcimer in place of drum machines. The records turned toward transition and loss.

years.cap: Mark Nelson performing as Pan American
years.p: Nelson wrote and recorded it at home in Evanston, then refined it on a European tour. The closer is a solo take on Shenandoah.
years.xp: According to Wikipedia, Nelson began playing Shenandoah after the 2017 Charlottesville attack as a tribute to Heather Heyer, the woman killed there. The Chicago Reader noted pieces for hammered dulcimer and guitar instrumentals in the spirit of Santo & Johnny.

q: I was looking at patience as a type of kindness.
years.h: Nelson records The Patience Fader at home as his father dies
years.p: He starts alone in spring 2020, during the pandemic. His father is dying that summer, and COVID limits Nelson to weekly FaceTime calls.
years.xp: There is no singing on the album. Nelson told Sun 13 the songs came out of his daily guitar practice rather than any theme.

years.p: [[Mimi Parker|31e0783a-9c5d-4218-9f23-4b9427b111e7]], who sang with [[Alan Sparhawk|36aa434c-6823-44b7-b5a6-53bde476c642]] on Pan American's 2000 album 360 Business/360 Bypass, dies of ovarian cancer.

eras.title: New partners, and a plane
eras.text: Nelson opened Pan American to partners: two albums with Kramer, founder of New York's Shimmy-Disc, and one with Michael Grigoni. Then came the most personal record yet, about parenthood, losing a parent and going home.

years.src: Pan•American on Bandcamp: Reverberations · Wikipedia: Shimmy-Disc
years.h: Pan American and Kramer make a record for the revived Shimmy-Disc
years.p: Reverberations of Non-Stop Traffic on Redding Road sets Nelson's guitar against Kramer's orchestral drones, pressed first as 555 hand-numbered LPs.
years.xp: [[Kramer|d898e082-70d1-4a86-ac8e-ecdf89892994]] founded Shimmy-Disc in New York in 1987 and revived it in 2020 with Joyful Noise Recordings. Nelson called the collaboration an honor.

years.h: A divided country, told in folk and blues forms
years.p: New World, Lonely Ride, made with Michael Grigoni, is an instrumental Kranky album about isolation. A second Kramer album, Interior of an Edifice Under the Sea, follows on Shimmy-Disc.

years.cap: Mark Nelson as Pan American at Big Ears Festival, Knoxville, March 27, 2026
q: one I never saw when she was alive
years.src: Pan•American on Bandcamp: Fly the Ocean in a Silver Plane · Style Weekly
years.h: On the cover, his mother looks ready to go somewhere
years.p: Fly the Ocean in a Silver Plane is Pan American's Kranky album about journeys, parenthood and losing a parent.
years.xp:
Nelson says the record grew from two songs about travel and coming home: Jo Stafford's You Belong to Me and Chuck Berry's Promised Land. He recorded it at home over several years on electric and rubber-bridge acoustic guitar, Ableton Live and a Digitone synth.

Mallory Linnehan of Chelsea Bridge added violin and vocals, recorded at the Not Not space in Chicago. Richmond's Style Weekly marked the release with a long interview.

Style Weekly asked what he wants the music to do. His answer was less about the listener while it plays than about leaving "a trace afterwards."
